name: Cornstarch Suspension (Oobleck)
use_case: Vertical plate vibration demonstration; shear-thickening Faraday-adjacent patterns

composition.notes: Exact ratio critical — 45% cornstarch produces runny suspension; 55% produces solid-like behaviour. 50/50 is the sweet spot for cymatic demonstrations.

rheology.mechanism: Under low stress: cornstarch particles are in quasi-liquid suspension. Under high stress (rapid vibration): the hydration shells between particles squeeze out and the particles jam together, forming a temporary solid.

behavior_at_sound.low_amplitude: Flows like thick cream; Faraday waves appear on surface
behavior_at_sound.medium_amplitude: Fingers and tendrils form — the surface 'grabs' and holds shapes between vibration cycles
behavior_at_sound.high_amplitude: Explosive — the surface erupts into standing pillars, fingers, and jets that appear to defy gravity (they solidify briefly on each compression stroke)
behavior_at_sound.special_phenomenon: At the right frequency and amplitude, stable standing columns form that look like living organisms. These are the most viscerally striking cymatic demonstration known.

notes: The cornstarch demonstration is NOT a Chladni figure — it does not form nodal lines. It is a demonstration of shear-thickening resonance where the acoustically-induced shear creates transient solidification patterns. Philosophically distinct from sand-plate cymatics but visually overwhelming.
safety: Non-toxic, fully edible. Extremely messy. Use over newspaper or in a rimmed tray. Blue food colouring improves visibility.
references: Merkt, F.S. et al. (2004). Long-lived Faraday wave patterns on a zero-mean-flow soap film. Physical Review Letters, 92(18).
Scott, A.B. (2004). Oobleck: The non-Newtonian fluid that dances to sound. Physics Teacher, 42, 414.
